extracted.intended_audience: IRB members, human-subjects researchers, legal scholars, and policymakers concerned with research regulation
extracted.subtask_short: IRB review of human subjects research
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and regulating risks, benefits, and definitional thresholds (e.g., 'research', 'minimal risk', 'human subjects') in human-subjects research; with emphasis on participant heterogeneity and its impact on IRB determinations. Includes examples of psychological, informational, and physical risks and regulatory constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizability as a criterion of 'research'
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizability is a core (but undefined) criterion in the Belmont Report and the Common Rule; whether an activity aims to produce generalizable knowledge affects whether it is 'research' subject to IRB review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether student projects or quality improvement/assurance activities are sufficiently 'generalizable' to fall within IRB jurisdiction is a perennial problem. Example: case studies defined by some institutions as not 'systemic investigation' and thus not exempt from IRB review; conversely, IRBs often treat student learning projects as requiring review when they appear intended to produce generalizable knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRB risk–benefit analysis steps (45 C.F.R. § 46.111(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a project's risks to subjects are reasonable in relation to anticipated benefits, IRBs must: (1) determine the magnitude of research-related harms and benefits to participants and the value of resulting knowledge; (2) discount these (dis)utilities by the probability they will occur; and (3) determine whether the resulting risks are 'reasonable in relation to' the project's aggregate expected benefits to participants and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technically, regulations suggest cataloguing harms/benefits irrespective of probability and then discounting, while the value of knowledge is counted only to the extent it is 'reasonably expected' to result. This requires IRBs to evaluate both probabilities and aggregate societal value and to balance them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation problem: single IRB determination for heterogeneous participants
rubrics_metrics.description: IRBs must make a single determination, applicable to all prospective participants, about a study's risks, expected benefits, and the reasonableness of the risk–benefit ratio despite participant heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because prospective participants vary in preferences, vulnerabilities, and perceptions of risk and benefit, IRB determinations may be arbitrary or may fail to capture individuals' private valuations. This aggregation challenge is central to evaluating studies where harms and benefits affect participants differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity of 'minimal risk'
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulatory definition of 'minimal risk' is notoriously ambiguous and often determines the kind of review a study receives or whether it is permissible at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'minimal risk' is unclear, IRBs vary in classifying studies (e.g., some IRBs consider certain adolescent sexual behavior surveys 'minimal', others consider them more than minimal). This classification has crucial regulatory consequences, especially for vulnerable populations (minors, prisoners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty over whether an activity involves 'human subjects'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Human subjects' status is 'not always straightforward' under the regulations, complicating IRB jurisdiction and review requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining whether an activity meets the regulatory definition of human subjects can be complex, especially for data-only projects, online participation, or secondary use of data; this uncertainty affects whether IRB scrutiny applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological risk: trauma research and risk of revictimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of traumatic experiences (sexual abuse, assault, disaster, war) can rekindle disturbing memories and cause significant psychological morbidity for some participants, creating risk of revictimization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs often respond by requiring mitigations (e.g., on-site counseling), which may alter study design and reduce generalizability (e.g., limiting an online survey to local administration). Empirical evidence shows most trauma-exposed individuals do not experience severe lasting distress, but a nontrivial minority do; IRBs differ in assessing seriousness of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological risk: sensitive topics (embarrassment, stigma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Research asking about socially disfavored or sensitive behaviors (drug use, sexual behavior, HIV status, criminal activity) may cause embarrassment, fear, or discomfort for participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs frequently restrict or slow research on such topics; examples include blocking sexuality-related research or demanding destruction of interview tapes. Empirical findings show average discomfort may be low but heterogeneous across subgroups (e.g., non-white respondents, recent drug users report greater discomfort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological risk: unpleasant self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Research that reveals potentially upsetting information to participants about themselves (e.g., possible alcoholism, rape victim status, implicit biases, genetic findings) can have both harmful and beneficial effects depending on the individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs sometimes prohibit or modify studies to avoid instigating distress (e.g., forcing explicit labeling as 'rape' or rejecting anonymous screenings). Reactions vary: some may be harmed, some may obtain net benefits (seek treatment, change behavior), others may dismiss results. The possibility of both harm and benefit complicates IRB decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informational privacy risk: disclosure of personally identifiable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Research can risk inadvertent disclosure of personally identifiable information; the likelihood of disclosure involves technical expertise, while the harm from disclosure depends on individual preferences and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals vary widely in privacy attitudes (correlates: gender, age, social media use) and these preferences can be unstable/context-dependent. Example: Personal Genome Project participants publicly share genomic and medical data despite general expectations of privacy. Proposed regulatory changes include assigning informational risk assessment to data-security/HIPAA standards rather than IRBs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical risk: heterogeneity in pain experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical harms (e.g., pain) show large interindividual and intraindividual variation—identical stimuli can produce widely different pain ratings across participants and over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SERR (Systematic Evaluation of Research Risks) uses dimensions such as 'experience, such as pain' to assess physical risk; empirical studies demonstrate pain ratings can range across full scales for identical stimuli, genetics explains part of variance, and gender/other factors can influence sensitivity depending on modality. IRBs should recognize variability even in physical risk assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of risk-assessment approaches to physical harms (SERR)
rubrics_metrics.description: SERR limits itself to assessing physical risks 'due to the[] strong context dependence' of economic and social harms, acknowledging that other harms are harder to quantify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While physical risk dimensions can be operationalized (e.g., pain intensity), economic, legal, and psychosocial harms are context-dependent and may resist standardized scoring, yet they remain important for IRB consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: IRB risk-management techniques can reduce research value and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions imposed by IRBs to mitigate risk (e.g., requiring on-site counselors, destroying data, restricting methods) can raise costs, limit generalizability, and effectively kill projects—particularly for unfunded researchers and students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: requiring on-site psychological counseling transformed an anonymous online survey into local administration, severely limiting generalizability, and high mitigation costs can prevent graduate students or small-scale researchers from conducting studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory constraints for vulnerable populations (minors, prisoners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal regulations impose stricter rules for research involving minors and prisoners; research that offers no prospect of direct benefit and is more than minimal risk may be unapprovable or require special approvals (e.g., 45 C.F.R. §§ 46.406, 46.407; Subpart C for prisoners).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IRBs must apply special regulatory categories: for children, more-than-minimal-risk research without direct benefit is generally not approvable except under narrow exceptions (minor increase over minimal risk plus knowledge about disorder, or Secretary-convened panel approval). Prisoner research typically permitted only if 'no more than minimal risk and no more than inconvenience.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant heterogeneity in risk perception correlated with demographics and status
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants' reported distress or privacy concerns vary systematically with demographic and situational factors (age, gender, insurance status, health status, race, prior trauma, recent illicit drug use, social media habits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show, for example, that trauma surveys generated higher upset rates among females, 45–64 age group, uninsured, those with probable PTSD/depression, and that non-white respondents or recent drug users report more discomfort to sensitive questions. IRBs should account for subgroup heterogeneity rather than assume homogeneous risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for technical expertise to estimate likelihood of informational disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating the probability of inadvertent disclosure of data requires technical (data-security, de-identification, re-identification risk) expertise that IRBs may lack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because IRBs often lack this expertise, proposals include removing such assessment from IRBs and requiring compliance with HIPAA/data-security standards for researchers, shifting the locus of assessment to technical compliance frameworks.
